name: Asthma attack
tagline: Wheezing that won't ease — act fast.

urgent.heading: Urgent — call now
urgent.primary_message: Use the blue reliever inhaler. If no improvement in 10 minutes — call 10177.
red_flags: Too breathless to speak in full sentences
Lips, fingernails, or face turning blue or grey
Chest sucks in between the ribs with each breath
Reliever inhaler not helping or wearing off in under 4 hours
Drowsiness, confusion, or exhaustion from breathing effort
Silent chest — wheeze stops because airflow is too low to make a sound

what_is_it.heading: Asthma attack in plain terms
what_is_it.lede: An asthma attack is when the airways in the lungs suddenly tighten, swell, and fill with mucus — making it hard to move air in and out.
paragraphs: Most asthma attacks have a trigger — a virus, smoke, pollen, dust, cold air, exercise, or emotional stress. The airway muscles spasm, the lining swells, and mucus clogs what's left of the airway.
A reliever inhaler (usually blue) relaxes the airway muscles within minutes. If it does not work, or if attacks are coming more often, the person needs urgent help — severe attacks can kill.

items.headline: 1 in 10
items.body: Roughly 1 in 10 South African children have asthma. Many adults have it without realising.

items.headline: Still kills
items.body: Hundreds of South Africans die of asthma every year — most deaths are preventable with proper treatment.

items.headline: Two inhalers
items.body: A blue reliever (used during attacks) and a brown preventer (used daily) — the preventer is what keeps you out of trouble.

items.headline: Live fully
items.body: Well-controlled asthma should not stop you from sport, school, work, or sleep. If it is — your treatment needs adjusting.

pull_quote.text: If you are reaching for your reliever inhaler more than twice a week, your asthma is not well controlled. See a doctor — do not just keep topping up the blue one.

signs.heading: What an attack looks like
signs.lede: Asthma attacks usually build over hours, sometimes over days. The earlier you treat, the easier it is to stop.

items.title: Wheezing
items.description: A whistling sound when breathing out, sometimes in. A silent chest in a severe attack means airflow has dropped dangerously low.

items.title: Shortness of breath
items.description: Struggling to get a full breath. Cannot finish a sentence without pausing. Chest feels tight.

items.title: Cough that won't stop
items.description: Dry, persistent cough, often worse at night or in the early morning. Sometimes the only symptom in children.

items.title: Body language
items.description: Hunched forward, shoulders raised, ribs pulling in with each breath, fast breathing, exhaustion.

myths.heading: What is true and what is not

items.fact: Some do, many do not. Even when symptoms settle, the airway sensitivity can return at any age. Keep the preventer inhaler going as prescribed.
Inhaled steroids in the brown preventer are very low dose and act locally in the lungs. They are far safer than the oral steroids needed when attacks get bad.

items.myth: If you can speak, the attack is not serious.
items.fact: Speech limited to short phrases — or single words — is a danger sign. A silent chest is worse, not better.

items.myth: Asthma medication is only needed when you feel symptoms.
items.fact: The preventer (brown) inhaler must be used every day, even when you feel fine. It controls the underlying inflammation that causes attacks.

action_steps.heading: What to do during an attack

items.title: Sit upright. Loosen tight clothing
items.description: Do not lie down. Sitting up with arms supported makes breathing easier. Stay calm — panic worsens breathing.

items.title: Use the blue reliever inhaler — 1 puff
items.description: Use a spacer if you have one. Wait 30 to 60 seconds. Repeat up to 10 puffs total in the first 10 minutes.

items.title: If no improvement in 10 minutes — call 10177
items.description: Say 'severe asthma attack'. Continue using the reliever every few minutes until paramedics arrive.

items.title: If they collapse or go blue — call immediately
items.description: Do not wait the 10 minutes. Severe attacks can become life-threatening fast.

items.title: After the attack — see a doctor
items.description: Every attack that needed more than the usual reliever dose is a sign your asthma plan needs adjustment. Do not skip the follow-up.

get_help.heading: Who to call
get_help.lede: If the blue inhaler is not working or attacks are getting more frequent, get help. Asthma is treatable.

helplines.name: Emergency (mobile)
helplines.description: Reaches any emergency service from a cellphone

helplines.name: Find your nearest clinic
helplines.description: Every government clinic provides asthma assessment and inhalers
